Flying to the UAE? These common medicines could land you in trouble

Flying to the UAE? These common medicines could land you in trouble

A new restriction takes effect November 1, but travellers face different rules

Last updated: October 21, 2026 | 06:00
Stacy Pereira, Business Reporter
3 MIN READ
Add as a preferred source on Google
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 3:42
Instaread

Dubai: The UAE will ban the veterinary use of ciprofloxacin, a widely prescribed antibiotic for pets and farm animals, from November 1. The ban was announced by the Emirates Drug Establishment (EDE) and will cover veterinary medicines and raw materials containing the drug. 

Nine products will get affected because of this ban. Eight of these are imported while one company is registered locally, and uses this drug. The latest development asks companies to stop making, importing and supplying the drug. It also asks them to clear existing stock before the deadline. Companies will have to re-exported the remaining stock or destroy it under approved procedures. 

While the ban addresses the companies importing or manufacturing the drug, it does not specify if the ban applies to pet medicine that can be procured outside and/or carried in personal luggage. For now, ciprofloxacin prescribed to people does not appear on the EDE’s controlled medicines list. 

Travelers face a different dilemma, which medicines can they carry during their travels to the UAE?

Get updated faster and for FREE: Download the Gulf News app now - simply click here.

Which medicines are banned and which are allowed 

Airlines like Emirates, Etihad and Air Arabia do not have a specified list of medicines that they prohibit from carrying on their aircrafts, but have a detailed list of prohibited and dangerous goods listed on their websites. But these airlines will follow the direction of the drug regulator, who has a detailed list, putting various drugs under three categories.

According to EDE’s controlled medicines list dated September 15, 2022, there are about 268 drugs that are either prohibited or allowed with a medical prescription.

Outright Ban

Heroin, cocaine, cannabis plant and resin, THC, synthetic cannabinoids, LSD, MDMA, mescaline, khat, psilocybin mushrooms, peyote and the opium poppy plant come under this list. Yohimbe bark and several fentanyl variants, such as 3-methylfentanyl, also fall here.  

Medicines allowed with a prescription or attested medical report:

Medicines on this list can be bought to the limit of the duration of stay or three months’ use, whichever is less. Emirates says controlled medication will need approval through the Ministry of Health website prior to travel. 

  • Opioid painkillers: codeine, tramadol, morphine, oxycodone, hydrocodone, methadone, fentanyl, pethidine 

  • Anti-anxiety drugs and sedatives: diazepam (Valium), alprazolam (Xanax), clonazepam, lorazepam, midazolam, temazepam

  • Sleep aids: zolpidem, zopiclone, zaleplon

  • Sleep aids: zolpidem, zopiclone, zaleplon

  • Nerve pain and seizure drugs: pregabalin, gabapentin, phenobarbital

  • ADHD and stimulants: methylphenidate, amfetamine, dexamfetamine, lisdexamfetamine

  • Others: pseudoephedrine, ephedrine, phentermine, buprenorphine, ketamine.

Allowed without prior approval:

Emirates says over-the-counter and uncontrolled prescription medicines need no approval. Paracetamol, ibuprofen, antihistamines, insulin, blood pressure tablets and antibiotics such as ciprofloxacin do not appear on the EDE list. Travellers can carry them in original packaging, with a prescription to be on the safe side.

Etihad Airlines also exempts prescription and non-prescription medicines, and medical items needed in flight. It specifies limits for powder on flights from Australia where passengers need to carry supporting evidence. Sealed, medically prescribed powders get a similar exemption on US flights. 

Similarly on Air Arabia a personal use mercury clinical thermometer can be carried per passenger in checked baggage, in a protective case. Oxygen cylinders are accepted only if they are approved medical cylinders that meet its conditions.

Travellers should check every medicine by its generic name, not the brand on the box, because the EDE list is written by active ingredient. Anyone unsure about a drug should contact the nearest UAE embassy or consulate before flying. A call to the airline can also clear up what is allowed in the cabin or in checked baggage. Carry prescriptions and original packaging, and leave enough time to apply for approval if the medicine is controlled.

UAE bans use of popular antibiotic for pets and farm animals from November 1

Ban covers nine veterinary medicinal products and raw materials: what you should know

Last updated: October 20, 2026 | 10:52
Sajila Saseendran
3 MIN READ
Add as a preferred source on Google

Dubai: The UAE is banning the use of ciprofloxacin, a popular antibiotic, in its veterinary sector from November 1, 2026, in a move aimed at tackling antimicrobial resistance.

The Emirates Drug Establishment (EDE) on Tuesday announced that the ban covers veterinary medicinal products and raw materials containing ciprofloxacin.

It affects nine veterinary products, including eight imported products and one locally registered product.

Ciprofloxacin belongs to the fluoroquinolone group of antibiotics. It is a strong antibiotic used to treat certain bacterial infections.

Get updated faster and for FREE: Download the Gulf News app now - simply click here.

Why the ban?

The decision is part of efforts to promote the safe use of antibiotics and preserve the effectiveness of treatments used in human medicine. It follows the classification of this group of antibiotics as Critically Important Antimicrobials (CIAs) for human medicine because of their role in treating certain bacterial infections.

Inappropriate use in animals could contribute to the development of bacterial resistance, potentially reducing the effectiveness of available treatments and posing a public health challenge.

The ban follows a scientific assessment of data related to antimicrobial resistance, including studies submitted by UAE University. The findings were used to support evidence-based regulatory decisions and strengthen national efforts to reduce the risks associated with antimicrobial resistance.

Risk-based approach

Dr Ruqaya Aqeel Al Bastaki, Acting Executive Director of the Medical Products Regulation Sector at the Emirates Drug Establishment, said regulating the use of antimicrobials requires an approach based on assessing the risks associated with each substance and how those risks affect treatment priorities across different sectors.

She explained that scientific evidence plays a key role in determining the appropriate level of regulatory intervention, allowing the establishment to take necessary measures when findings point to risks that require action, taking into account the nature of each substance and its uses.

Al Bastaki added that the establishment is committed to keeping its decisions aligned with the latest scientific developments and responding proactively to risks linked to antimicrobial resistance.

These efforts aim to preserve the effectiveness of available treatments, strengthen pharmaceutical security, ensure the sustainability of medical products and protect public health.

The decision falls within the Emirates Drug Establishment's mandate to regulate the use of medical and pharmaceutical products and monitor compliance with the relevant approved requirements.

What companies must do

Ahead of the ban's implementation, the establishment has taken the necessary regulatory steps to identify the products and raw materials covered by the decision.

It has notified the relevant establishments that they must stop manufacturing, importing and supplying these products, withdraw existing quantities from the local market before the ban takes effect, and either re-export or dispose of remaining stocks in accordance with approved procedures.

Establishments must also submit supporting documents confirming that the required measures have been completed.

EDE is also preparing a monitoring plan to assess compliance with the decision and verify that the relevant establishments complete the required procedures within the specified timeframe.

The decision was taken as part of the Emirates Drug Establishment's efforts to strengthen oversight of veterinary medical products, promote the responsible use of antimicrobials and support national initiatives to combat antimicrobial resistance, helping protect human and animal health while strengthening the UAE's public health system, EDE said.

Flying Emirates, Etihad, flydubai or Air Arabia? What you can and can’t pack in your baggage

Flying from the UAE during the holiday season? Check these baggage rules before you pack

Last updated: October 05, 2026 | 13:30
Lekshmy Pavithran
6 MIN READ
Add as a preferred source on Google

Heading abroad from the UAE this holiday season? One wrongly packed power bank, liquid or prohibited item could leave you repacking your suitcase at the airport — or having it confiscated.

The holiday travel season is one of the busiest times of the year, with thousands of UAE residents flying abroad for vacations, family visits and winter breaks.

Airlines have strict rules on what passengers can carry in cabin and checked baggage, covering everything from batteries and electronics to food, medicines, aerosols and sports equipment. Rules can also vary by airline, destination and transit point.

Get updated faster and for FREE: Download the Gulf News app now - simply click here.

Here’s a practical guide to what you can pack, what needs special handling — and what you should leave at home.

Emirates: What you can’t pack

Emirates bans explosives, dangerous chemicals and other hazardous items from both cabin and checked baggage.

Banned items

  • Fireworks and explosives

  • Pepper spray, mace and stun devices

  • Dangerous chemicals and hazardous substances

  • Hoverboards, mini-Segways and smart balance wheels

  • Smart bags with non-removable batteries

Cabin baggage

Large knives, axes, drills and saws cannot be carried in cabin baggage.

E-cigarettes and personal vaporizers are allowed only in cabin baggage and must be protected against accidental activation.

Power banks and batteries

  • Only one power bank up to 100Wh is allowed.

  • It must be kept in cabin baggage and not in the overhead locker.

  • It cannot be used or charged during the flight.

  • Spare or loose lithium batteries must be carried in cabin baggage and protected against short circuits.

  • Emirates allows up to 20 spare batteries, subject to applicable limits.

Drones are not allowed in cabin baggage but may be accepted in checked baggage, subject to battery rules.

Food and liquids

  • Cabin liquids, gels, creams, pastes and drinks must generally be in containers of 100ml or less and fit into one transparent, resealable 1-litre bag.

  • Baby food and milk, medicines and special dietary items may qualify for exemptions.

  • Travellers flying to, from or through the US, Australia or New Zealand can face additional restrictions on powders.

  • Alcohol between 24% and 70% ABV is permitted within Emirates’ limits. Alcohol above 70% ABV is prohibited.

Etihad: What you can’t pack

Etihad applies different restrictions depending on the item and whether it is carried in the cabin or checked baggage.

Sharp objects and weapons

  • Safety or disposable razors with enclosed blades are permitted in cabin baggage; other razors must go in checked baggage.

  • Toy guns and toy weapons are not allowed in the cabin.

  • Spear guns and harpoons require advance approval and permits.

  • Cremated remains cannot be carried in cabin baggage but may be accepted in checked baggage or as cargo with the required documentation.

Power banks and batteries

  • Spare batteries and power banks must not be placed in checked baggage.

  • They must be carried in the cabin and individually protected.

  • Lithium-ion batteries up to 100Wh are permitted within Etihad’s limits.

  • Batteries between 100Wh and 160Wh require authorisation.

  • Batteries above 160Wh are not accepted.

  • Power banks cannot be used or charged onboard.

E-cigarettes, e-pipes and personal vaporizers must be carried in cabin baggage.

Smart bags with a non-removable battery or power bank are not accepted.

Drones

Drones may be carried subject to battery restrictions.

  • Batteries must not exceed 160Wh.

  • Up to two spare drone batteries can be carried in cabin baggage if individually protected.

  • Drones with non-removable batteries whose capacity cannot be verified will not be accepted.

Food

Solid food can generally be carried if properly packed. However, soups, sauces, jams, stews and pastes are treated as liquids or gels and are subject to the 100ml cabin limit.

Etihad also bans strong-smelling perishables such as:

  • Durian

  • Champedek

  • Pedalai

  • Marang

  • Jackfruit

Fruit and vegetables may also be restricted depending on the destination.

Zamzam and cooking oils

Passengers travelling from Jeddah with an Umrah or Haj visa can carry Zamzam water subject to Etihad’s requirements:

  • Up to 100ml in cabin baggage

  • Up to 5 litres in checked baggage, when suitably packaged

Cooking and olive oil are subject to separate packaging and quantity limits.

flydubai: What you can’t pack

flydubai bans a wide range of dangerous goods from both cabin and checked baggage.

Banned in all baggage

  • Pepper spray, mace and Tasers

  • Fireworks, flares and explosives

  • Ammunition

  • Petrol, diesel and lighter fluid

  • Butane, propane and other flammable gases

  • Poisons and insecticides

  • Corrosive chemicals

  • Acids, bleaches and peroxides

  • Fertilisers and weed killers

  • Radioactive or magnetised materials

  • Damaged, defective or recalled batteries and electronic devices

  • Lithium batteries exceeding 160Wh

  • Realistic toy guns and weapon replicas

  • Hoverboards and self-balancing devices

  • Motorised rideable suitcases

  • Firearms and other weapons

Any item prohibited by the country of departure, transit or arrival is also not accepted.

What cannot go in hand baggage

Many sharp objects, tools and sporting equipment must stay out of the cabin.

Examples include:

  • Knives, scissors and box cutters

  • Corkscrews and knitting needles

  • Screwdrivers, drills, hammers and saws

  • Golf clubs, bats and hockey sticks

  • Axes and ice picks

  • Ski and hiking poles

  • Bows and arrows

  • Nunchakus, batons and swords

  • Stun guns

  • Fishing rods

  • Glue guns

  • Ropes and luggage chains

  • Handcuffs

  • Non-toiletry aerosols

Passengers can carry one box of matches or one lighter, subject to flydubai’s conditions.

Liquids and aerosols

Cabin liquids, gels, pastes, creams and aerosols must generally:

  • Be in containers of 100ml or less

  • Fit into one transparent, resealable bag

  • Be packed in a bag no larger than 20cm x 20cm

  • Stay within a maximum total capacity of 1 litre

Baby food and essential medical or special-dietary liquids may qualify for exemptions, subject to screening.

Toiletry and medicinal aerosols have an additional limit of 2kg or 2 litres, with each item limited to 0.5kg or 0.5 litre.

Air Arabia: What you can’t pack

Air Arabia also restricts dangerous goods, batteries, aerosols and other items. It allows passengers to choose their checked baggage allowance when booking or modifying a flight.

Power banks and batteries

  • Spare or loose batteries must be carried in cabin baggage only.

  • Lithium-metal batteries must not exceed 2g of lithium.

  • Lithium-ion batteries must not exceed 100Wh.

  • Passengers can carry a maximum of two power banks, each up to 100Wh.

  • Power banks must be kept in cabin baggage, not in the overhead locker.

  • They must be stored in the seat pocket or inside a bag that fits under the seat.

  • Power banks cannot be used or charged during the flight.

  • E-cigarettes and personal vaporizers are permitted only in cabin baggage.

Banned items

Air Arabia prohibits items including:

  • Pepper spray, mace and disabling sprays

  • Tasers and other electro-shock weapons

  • Strike-anywhere matches

  • Blue-flame and cigar lighters

  • Firearms and explosives

  • Flammable fuels and paints

  • Butane and propane

  • Poisons such as insecticides and weed killers

  • Corrosive substances

  • Infectious materials

  • Radioactive and oxidising materials

Hoverboards, electric skateboards, Segways, self-balancing scooters and similar rideable devices are also prohibited because of their large lithium batteries.

Checked baggage

Power banks, spare batteries, e-cigarettes and personal vaporizers cannot be packed in checked baggage.

Personal electronic devices can be placed in checked baggage if they are completely switched off and protected from damage.

Toiletries and aerosols are permitted within these limits:

  • Maximum 2kg or 2 litres per passenger

  • Each item must not exceed 0.5kg or 0.5 litre

  • Aerosol valves must be protected against accidental release

Air Arabia cabin baggage allowance

Passengers can carry:

  • 1 cabin bag: maximum 55 × 40 × 20cm and up to 7kg

  • 1 personal item: maximum 25 × 33 × 20cm and up to 3kg

  • Duty-free purchases, provided the combined cabin allowance does not exceed 10kg

Passengers travelling with an infant under two can carry one additional small bag of up to 3kg for baby essentials.

Liquids over 100ml, sharp objects and flammable materials are not permitted in cabin baggage.

Checked baggage allowance

Air Arabia offers three pre-booked options:

  • 20kg: maximum one piece

  • 30kg: maximum two pieces

  • 40kg: maximum two pieces

Each checked bag must not exceed 32kg or 158cm in total dimensions.

Availability and fees vary by route. Buying baggage at the airport may also cost more than pre-booking.

Food: Check your destination rules

Taking snacks or homemade food on a holiday trip? Airline rules are only part of the picture.

  • Solid food is generally easier to carry than liquids or gels.

  • Soups, sauces, jams and pastes can fall under cabin liquid restrictions.

  • Meat and dairy products may be restricted at your destination.

  • Fresh fruit, vegetables, seeds and other agricultural products may be prohibited or require declaration.

  • Customs rules can be stricter than airline rules.

For example, Etihad specifically prohibits strong-smelling perishables such as durian and jackfruit.

Holiday travel: 5 things to check before packing

  • Check your airline: Emirates, Etihad, flydubai and Air Arabia have different baggage rules.

  • Check cabin vs checked baggage: An item allowed in checked baggage may be banned from the cabin — and vice versa.

  • Keep power banks in your cabin bag: Spare lithium batteries and power banks generally cannot go in checked baggage.

  • Check your destination: Customs rules can restrict food, medicines, agricultural products and other items even if your airline permits them.

  • Check before you leave home: Rules can depend on the item, battery capacity, packaging, route and destination.

Holiday tip: Don’t wait until you reach the airport to discover that a power bank, food item, aerosol or sharp object has to be removed from your bag. Check your airline’s latest baggage rules before you travel.

India to UAE flights: Food, medicines and other items you cannot bring in 2026

Avoid surprises at the airport - These items Indian travellers can’t bring on flights

Last updated: August 03, 2026 | 08:28
Zainab Husain
3 MIN READ
Add as a preferred source on Google

Dubai: When travelling to the UAE or to any other country, it is important to check the list of restricted or banned items before you start packing. Like other countries, the UAE has regulations on what can and cannot be brought in, including certain foods, vapes, e-cigarettes, and medication.

In addition, airlines and aviation authorities in the UAE enforce strict rules on carrying batteries, power banks, drones, and flammable items, as these are considered safety hazards and are severely restricted.

For many Indian expatriates returning to the UAE after the summer break, or visitors travelling from India to the UAE, it is common to bring home-made or locally sourced delicacies. However, Indian airlines must follow the guidelines issued by the Bureau of Civil Aviation Security (BCAS), meaning that some items are restricted and, in some cases, banned.

While certain goods may be permitted in checked baggage, they may not be allowed in your carry-on luggage. Some of these items are restricted because they have a high oil content or are easily combustible in the air.

Food items banned or restricted on flights from India to the UAE

  • Copra (dried coconut) – Prohibited

  • Coconut crushed (dry coconut) – Prohibited

  • All spices in powder/physical form, including chilli – Carry-on: No Check-in: Yes

  • Coconut – Carry-on: No, Check-in: Yes

  • Coconut crushed (green tissue) – Allowed in both carry-on and check-in

  • Ghee (clarified butter) / cooking oil – Allowed in both. Note: Allowed in cabin baggage as per LAG restrictions; in checked baggage, the quantity is limited to 5 kg/l per passenger.

  • Pickle – Allowed in both. Note: Chilli pickle is only allowed in checked-in baggage.

Personal food can be brought into the UAE’s borders, but there are restrictions on certain types and quantities. According to Dubai Customs, items such as paan (betel leaves) or cooked food items are not allowed into the UAE.

Other restricted items

In addition to food and medication restrictions, Indian travellers flying to the UAE should also be aware that certain items are prohibited or restricted in baggage, including:

  • Poppy seeds

  • Strong-smelling food items like Durian, champedek, pedalai, marang and jackfruit

  • Cricket bats, skateboards and fishing rods

  • Measuring tapes are prohibited in carry-on baggage.

  • Toy guns and imitation weapons

  • Bows and arrows

  • Weapons and weapon replicas

  • Knives with blades measuring 6 cm or longer

  • Explosives and ammunition, including fireworks and firecrackers

Medication rules for travellers from India to the UAE

All travellers carrying controlled medication into the UAE must apply for approval through the Ministry of Health and Prevention (MoHAP) website before making the trip.

Check with your doctor to confirm whether your prescribed medication is controlled. You must also carry the prescription for the quantity of medicine you are bringing into the UAE.

For all other medication (prescriptions for uncontrolled medication and over-the-counter medicines), prior approval from MoHAP is not required.

Travellers to the UAE are strongly advised to familiarise themselves with what medications they can and cannot bring into the country. Contact the nearest UAE embassy or consulate for advice if you are considering taking medications or other drugs into the UAE.

Here is a link to all the UAE missions abroad and their contact details: www.mofa.gov.ae/en/missions/uae-missions-abroad.

Narcotic drugs and illegal substances

The UAE strictly prohibits passengers from bringing narcotic drugs and illegal substances into the country. Items such as hashish, cocaine, heroin, poppy seeds, and hallucinogenic pills are banned and cannot be carried in luggage.

Travellers should not attempt to carry any narcotic or psychotropic substances unless they have the required approvals for authorised medical use. The UAE has strict regulations on controlled substances, and certain medicines containing controlled ingredients require prior approval before travel.

Important note: This article is for informational purposes only. Always check with your airline before travelling if you are unsure about carrying certain items or medication, as customs and aviation regulations can be updated at any time.

Emirates, Etihad, flydubai, Air Arabia powerbank rules passengers must know before flying

UAE airlines ban the use of power banks during flights

Last updated: July 28, 2026 | 13:08
Dhanusha Gokulan
4 MIN READ
Add as a preferred source on Google

Dubai: A power bank that caught fire on board a commercial flight in China has once again highlighted why airlines are tightening rules on carrying and using portable chargers.

Sign up for our daily business newsletter, Cheques & Balances.

The latest incident occurred aboard China Eastern Airlines Flight MU2421 on July 24 after the aircraft landed at Guiyang Longdongbao International Airport. According to the South China Morning Post, the power bank inside a passenger’s carry-on bag caught fire while the Airbus A320 was taxiing to the terminal.

Cabin crew quickly extinguished the flames before anyone was injured, although the aircraft sustained minor smoke damage.

Videos shared online showed smoke and flames coming from an overhead baggage compartment as crew members responded.

The incident serves as a timely reminder for travellers flying from the UAE, where major airlines have introduced strict rules governing how power banks must be carried and stored onboard.

Why are airlines concerned?

Power banks contain lithium-ion or lithium-polymer batteries. If these batteries become damaged, overheat or develop an internal fault, they can enter a process known as thermal runaway, where temperatures rise rapidly and may lead to fire.

Because of this risk, airlines require power banks to remain inside the aircraft cabin, where cabin crew can respond immediately if something goes wrong.

Several UAE carriers also prohibit passengers from using power banks during flights.

Emirates: One power bank only

Emirates introduced new power bank restrictions that came into effect on October 1, 2025, following what it described as a comprehensive safety review.

Passengers may carry one power bank with a maximum capacity of 100 watt-hours (Wh).

However, the airline prohibits:

  • Using a power bank to charge phones, tablets or laptops during the flight.

  • Charging the power bank using the aircraft's USB ports or power sockets.

  • Storing the power bank inside an overhead baggage compartment.

  • Packing power banks inside checked baggage.

Instead, passengers must keep the device in the seat pocket or inside a bag stored beneath the seat in front of them, allowing cabin crew quick access if an emergency occurs.

Emirates also requires the battery's capacity rating to be clearly visible on the device.

Etihad: Keep it within reach

Etihad Airways has similar requirements.

Passengers may carry one power bank of up to 100Wh, provided the watt-hour rating is clearly marked.

The Abu Dhabi carrier says passengers must not:

  • Use the power bank onboard.

  • Charge the power bank.

  • Use it to charge other electronic devices.

The airline also recommends storing the device somewhere easily accessible.

Economy passengers should place it in a bag under the seat or in the seat pocket, while First and Business Class passengers should use the seat's storage compartment. Etihad advises travellers not to place power banks in overhead lockers because they may not be immediately accessible during an emergency.

Power banks exceeding 100Wh are not permitted.

Also Read: Emirates issues travel advisory ahead of summer rush at DXB

flydubai: Lithium battery limits apply

According to flydubai's dangerous goods guidance, lithium batteries exceeding 160Wh or containing more than 8g of lithium are prohibited.

According to the flydubai passenger guide, travellers may carry one power bank with a maximum capacity of 100Wh in their hand baggage only. The airline prohibits passengers from using a power bank to charge devices or recharging the power bank during the flight.

The device must remain switched off throughout the journey and be stored either in the seat pocket or inside hand baggage placed under the seat in front, rather than in the overhead locker.

Power banks are not permitted in checked baggage, and batteries with a capacity exceeding 160Wh are not allowed on board.

Also Read: Saudi Arabia bans charging power banks onboard flights

Air Arabia: Strict cabin-only policy

Air Arabia treats power banks as spare lithium batteries.

The airline requires passengers to:

  • Carry power banks in cabin baggage only.

  • Never place them in checked baggage.

  • Store them in the seat pocket or under the seat rather than in overhead lockers.

  • Keep them switched off throughout the flight.

  • Not use them to charge electronic devices onboard.

  • Not charge them using the aircraft's power supply.

Like Emirates and Etihad, Air Arabia permits lithium-ion power banks only if they do not exceed 100Wh.

What international airlines are saying

The tighter airline policies reflect a broader push by the aviation industry to improve lithium battery safety.

In its updated 2026 guidance, the International Air Transport Association (IATA) said airlines are moving ahead with stricter measures on power banks following recent safety incidents, even before the proposed rules are formally adopted.

The guidance recommends limiting passengers to two power banks of up to 100Wh each, prohibits charging them using the aircraft's power supply, advises against storing them in overhead lockers, and says they should not be used during taxi, take-off or landing.

Airlines may also impose stricter requirements.

What US's FAA says

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) bans portable power banks from checked luggage due to fire risks, requiring them to be carried in the cabin, even if bags are gate-checked.

Power banks up to 100 Watt-hours (Wh) are permitted, while those between 101 Wh and 160 Wh require airline approval, and those exceeding 160 Wh are prohibited.

Furthermore, all portable power sources must have their terminals protected to prevent short-circuits, with some carriers requiring they remain under the seat for monitoring.

Bottom line for travellers

While each airline has its own detailed dangerous goods policy, the message from UAE carriers is largely consistent: carry power banks in your cabin baggage, keep them within easy reach, never pack them in checked luggage, and do not use them during the flight where prohibited.

The latest onboard fire involving a portable charger is another reminder that even everyday electronic accessories are subject to strict aviation safety rules designed to reduce the risk of lithium battery fires.
